answer:
Let the unit square be \(0\le x\le 1,\;0\le y\le 1\), and take the left edge to be \(x=0\). The horizontal edges are \(y=0\) and \(y=1\).

## 1. Distance to the left edge

For \(P=(x,y)\),

\[
d_{\text{left}}=x,\qquad d_{\text{bottom}}=y,\qquad d_{\text{top}}=1-y.
\]

The condition is that \(d_{\text{left}}\) is smaller than both horizontal distances:

\[
x<y \quad\text{and}\quad x<1-y.
\]

Thus

\[
y>x,\qquad y<1-x.
\]

So the colored region is

\[
x<y<1-x.
\]

This requires \(x<\frac12\). Geometrically it is the triangle bounded by the two diagonals from the left corners to the center of the square. Its vertices are

\[
(0,0),\qquad (0,1),\qquad \left(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\right).
\]

The base is the left side of length \(1\), and the height to the center is \(\frac12\). Hence

\[
A_1=\frac12\cdot 1\cdot \frac12=\boxed{\frac14}.
\]

Boundary points do not affect the area.

---

## 2. Replace left edge by the lower-left corner

Now take the lower-left corner to be \(C=(0,0)\). For \(P=(x,y)\),

\[
d_C(P)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.
\]

The distance to the bottom horizontal edge is \(y\), and the distance to the top horizontal edge is \(1-y\). We would need

\[
\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<y
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<1-y.
\]

But already the first inequality is impossible in the square, because

\[
\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ge y
\]

with equality only when \(x=0\). Therefore no point is strictly closer to the lower-left corner than to the bottom edge. Geometrically, the locus equidistant from \((0,0)\) and the bottom edge \(y=0\) is the degenerate parabola

\[
x^2+y^2=y^2 \implies x=0,
\]

namely the left edge itself; off that edge every point is farther from the corner than from the bottom edge.

Hence the colored set has area

\[
A_2=\boxed{0}.
\]

So the colored area changes from

\[
\boxed{\frac14 \text{ to } 0}.
\]

If one used non-strict “at most” inequalities, the second case would include at most a line segment on the left edge, which still has area \(0\).
